ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Participants were recruited from primary care clinics across the Mount Sinai Health System without specific inclusion criteria, thus providing a cohort broadly representative of the New York City population and its neighborhood.

> Genetic ancestries of MSM participants were inferred using HapMap3 populations as a reference 10 .

> In brief, 6,814 participants that were free of overt cardiovascular disease (aged 45-84 years old that were self-reported as White, Black, Hispanic, or Chinese) were recruited and enrolled across the U.S. with exam 1 occurring from 2000-2002.

> Genetic ancestries of UK Biobank participants were inferred using PCA and ADMIXTURE 71, and 180,500 EUR samples were included in the analyses.

> The Mount Sinai Million Health Discoveries Program data used in the study was accessed with approval from the Institutional Review Board at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai (STUDY-20-00338), and all participants provided informed consent.

Ethics approval statement:

> The Mount Sinai Million Health Discoveries Program data used in the study was accessed with approval from the Institutional Review Board at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai (STUDY-20-00338), and all participants provided informed consent.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("P = 0.82", "P = 0.31"), Sentence = c("Mendelian randomization analyses, however, did not find significant evidence for a causal effect of circulating vanin-1 levels on BMI (β = -0.0006, SE = 0.003, P = 0.82) or for whole body fat mass (β = -0.003, SE = 0.003, P = 0.31).", "Mendelian randomization analyses, however, did not find significant evidence for a causal effect of circulating vanin-1 levels on BMI (β = -0.0006, SE = 0.003, P = 0.82) or for whole body fat mass (β = -0.003, SE = 0.003, P = 0.31)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

#### README Files

README files are a way to document the contents and structure of a folder, helping users locate the information they need. You can use a README to document changes to a repository, and explain how files are named. Please consider adding a README to each repository or including 'README' in the name of your overview document.

#### Archive Files

The following files are not ZIP archives: LoGoFuncVotingEnsemble_preds_final.csv.gz. We recommend the `.zip` format for archives: only ZIP stores its file listing in a way that lets a tool inspect the contents without downloading the whole archive, so a `.zip` is more discoverable and re-usable than a `.7z`, `.rar`, `.tar` or `.tar.gz`.

#### Unclassified Files

We could not classify 58 files by name or extension: model_0.joblib, model_1.joblib, model_10.joblib, model_11.joblib, model_12.joblib, model_13.joblib, model_14.joblib, model_15.joblib, model_16.joblib, model_17.joblib. Add a recognisable keyword (`data`, `code`, `materials`, `documentation`, `output`) to the file name, or use a common extension, so both humans and machines can tell what kind of file it is.

#### Study/Repository Mismatch

The studies named in the manuscript do not match how the repository's files are grouped: the manuscript names a study (ex20) with no matching files in the repository; the repository separates out studies (ex1, ex2) not named in the manuscript. Check that every study has its own clearly-named folder or file prefix, and that the folder names match how the manuscript refers to each study.
#### File Naming

File names should be machine-parseable: no spaces or special characters, and every file should be classifiable by name or extension. We found 58 naming problems that should be fixed, and 10 files with a naming suggestion (not required, but a good habit).

#### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 32 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: compiled Python files (6), version control (26). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 2008 columns across 8 data files.
#### Issues Identified

4 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = c("data/X_test_id.csv", "data/X_train_id.csv", "logofunc.zip/logofunc/data/X_test_id.csv", "logofunc.zip/logofunc/data/X_train_id.csv" ), Column = c("SiPhy_29way_logOdds", "SiPhy_29way_logOdds", "SiPhy_29way_logOdds", "SiPhy_29way_logOdds"), Issues = c("🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Column name suggests personal information (matched: ip)", "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Column name suggests personal information (matched: ip)", "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Column name suggests personal information (matched: ip)", "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Column name suggests personal information (matched: ip)" )), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 8 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Participants were recruited from primary care clinics across the Mount Sinai Health System without specific inclusion criteria, thus providing a cohort broadly representative of the New York City population and its neighborhood.
Genetic ancestries of MSM participants were inferred using HapMap3 populations as a reference 10 .

In brief, 6,814 participants that were free of overt cardiovascular disease (aged 45-84 years old that were self-reported as White, Black, Hispanic, or Chinese) were recruited and enrolled across the U.S. with exam 1 occurring from 2000-2002.
Genetic ancestries of UK Biobank participants were inferred using PCA and ADMIXTURE 71, and 180,500 EUR samples were included in the analyses.

The Mount Sinai Million Health Discoveries Program data used in the study was accessed with approval from the Institutional Review Board at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai (STUDY-20-00338), and all participants provided informed consent.

report: ### Python code
This module also assesses whether the paper's Python code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 6 Python code files.
#### Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first) and numeric filename prefixes. Python has no `source()`-equivalent import-based ordering signal (an `import` loads a module, not the paper's own analysis flow), so that basis never applies here.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:6, File = c("scripts/__init__.py", "logofunc.zip/logofunc/scripts/__init__.py", 
"train.py", "predict.py", "test.py", "utils.py"), "Runs after" = c("—", 
"—", "—", "train.py", "train.py", "—"), Basis = c("none", 
"none", "none", "dependency", "dependency", "none")), row.names = c(NA, 
-6L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

**1 data path in the code does not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed it to where the file is, so the code could run: `/preprocessor.joblib` to `models/preprocessor.joblib` (in predict.py). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find the file.
#### Files not run on their own
2 files are not part of the analysis but of software (a package, its tests or documentation, a tool, a web application), so they were not run or counted as scripts.
#### Execution

**The Python code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 4 scripts: 0 ran without error, 2 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 0 are written for Python 2 and not run. 1 file was not run on its own, because other files import it: utils.py (by predict.py, test.py, train.py). Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions (e.g. in a `requirements.txt`).

reproducibility_check.checklist_section: We ran the paper's 3 Python scripts in the order they depend on each other, each in an isolated container, for at most 5 minutes per script. 4 identical copies of these scripts, which other links in the paper lead to, were not run again. **0 of 3 scripts ran to the end**: 2 stopped with an error, 1 needed a person. | Script | Result | What happened | |---|---|---| | scripts/__init__.py | Not run | It makes its folder a Python package that other files import; it is not a script. | | logofunc.zip/logofunc/scripts/__init__.py | Not run | It makes its folder a Python package that other files import; it is not a script. | | train.py | Stopped with an error | TypeError: OneHotEncoder.__init__() got an unexpected keyword argument 'sparse' | | predict.py | Stopped | It asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, starts an app, or is a program that needs its arguments. | | test.py | Stopped with an error | AttributeError: 'SimpleImputer' object has no attribute 'keep_empty_features' | | utils.py | Ran inside another script | Another script imports it, so it ran as part of that script. | ### How to make your code run on another computer We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it. **A script waits for a person to choose a file, answer a question, or give arguments on the command line.** - predict.py Nobody can answer when the code is checked automatically. Write the file name into the script, and put the exact command with its arguments in the README. **Metacheck can't automatically establish what caused the error, or how it should be improved.** - train.py - test.py The error message of each script is in the table above. ### Comparison with the paper We found no statistical tests in the paper to compare with the output of the code.
